tier_reason: PLDI 2020 paper (read via the author's gaoxiang9430.github.io repo PDF, Section 6.1) measures E9Patch on SPEC2006 on a Xeon Silver 4114 with the default system gcc/g++/gfortran: +110.81% overhead for jump-instruction patching (A1) and +64.71% for heap-write patching (A2). It then cites, from the other tools' own papers, about 70% for Dyninst basic-block counting, +62% for PEBIL and +60.48% for Multiverse, and says those inlining rewriters generally perform better; E9Patch's argument is robustness and scalability, not speed.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No speedup over Dyninst. PLDI 2020 paper, SPEC2006: E9Patch adds +110.81% runtime overhead for patching all jump instructions (A1) and +64.71% for heap writes (A2); the paper cites about 70% for Dyninst basic-block counting, +62% for PEBIL and +60.48% for Multiverse (cited from those tools' papers, not measured side by side) and says those inlining rewriters generally give better performance. Chrome +113%, Firefox +46% on Dromaeo. README: the current -O2 mode is sometimes 2x faster than the PLDI prototype (self-comparison).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: SPEC2006 built with Ubuntu 16.04 default gcc/g++/gfortran, non-PIE; flags not stated
corrections.caveats: Not faster than the baseline: by its own paper E9Patch has higher overhead than Dyninst, PEBIL and Multiverse, trading speed for not needing control-flow recovery and for scaling to Chrome/Firefox. The baseline numbers are cited from other papers, not run side by side. Dyninst is not in this category's baseline list. The README says the current version with -O2 is sometimes 2x faster than the evaluated prototype, so the paper numbers may overstate today's overhead. GPL-3.0 with some files MIT.

notes: Paper reached through raw.githubusercontent.com/gaoxiang9430/gaoxiang9430.github.io (papers/PLDI20.pdf). Rejected as not-faster under the verifier rules; if the keep-and-document rule applies, keep it flagged as slower than Dyninst. Metadata checked: 1.2k stars, GPL-3.0, last commit 2026-06-28.

tier_reason: The 3x-faster-than-Valgrind-memcheck (80% more bugs, SPEC CPU2006 C benchmarks) and 4.5x-over-QEMU claims come from the IEEE S&P 2020 abstract and appear the same way in several WebSearch snippets, but the paper and thesis PDFs (nebelwelt.net, hexhive.epfl.ch) are blocked and no copy exists on GitHub. The repo has no numbers, so this is capped at C on snippet-only evidence until the paper is read.

corrections.claimed_speedup: IEEE S&P 2020 abstract (via search snippets): binary-only ASan 3x faster than Valgrind memcheck on SPEC CPU2006 C benchmarks while detecting 80% more bugs; AFL coverage instrumentation as fast as compiler instrumentation and 4.5x faster than QEMU-mode AFL; fuzzing throughput 4.2x (real-world) and 5.6x (LAVA-M) over QEMU AFL.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from abstract snippets only; the paper (nebelwelt.net/files/20Oakland.pdf, hexhive.epfl.ch) is blocked by egress and the README makes only a qualitative zero-overhead claim, so CPU, compiler and per-benchmark numbers were not checked. Retier candidate to B once the paper is reachable. The tool is written in Python, but its output is instrumented x86_64/aarch64 binaries. x64 rewriting needs PIC/PIE binaries; aarch64 uses a different algorithm (thesis). Last commit 2025-04-26.

notes: The paper is a retier candidate (C to B) once nebelwelt.net or hexhive.epfl.ch is reachable. Metadata matches the record: MIT, 751 stars, last commit 2025-04-26 (stale).

tier_reason: The first-party wiki comparison table gives typical slowdowns of ASan 2x, Valgrind/Memcheck 20x and Dr. Memory 10x, with no methodology. The separate SPEC CPU2006 page (Xeon W3690, clang 3.3 r179094 -O2) has ASan-only numbers (1.93 average, 1.86 median) and no Valgrind column, so this is C.

corrections.license: Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception (LICENSE.TXT; legacy compiler-rt code dual NCSA/MIT)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang 3.3 trunk r179094, -O2 baseline vs -O2 -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer (SPEC numbers page)
corrections.caveats: README says the repo is archived and no longer maintained; recent commits are buildbot infrastructure, and the ASan code lives in llvm/llvm-project compiler-rt (canonical code repo). The Valgrind comparison is a first-party rounded 'typical slowdown' table with no hardware or compiler; the hardware and compiler above belong to the separate SPEC page, which has no Valgrind column. Numbers date from 2013. ASan does not detect uninitialized reads (Memcheck does; that is MemorySanitizer's job), so the tools do not cover the same bugs.
